newsitem.title: UK: Euro Crude Outlook - June stragglers hold market bac.
newsitem.headline: Euro Crude Outlook - June stragglers hold market bac.

text.p: Europe's crude buyers were facing a relaxed week as West African and North Sea markets remained awash with unsold June loading barrels, traders said on Monday.

Depressed U.S. markets, where prompt NYMEX futures slid to a 16-month low on Friday under the weight of heavy inventories, would also offer little in the way of relief for sellers searching for custom.
"I see Brent softer, and likewise for the other (North Sea) grades," a trader said.
"There is ample availability and the arbitrage to the States is not good."
The prompt Brent/WTI spread was pegged at $1.17 a barrel, making it difficult for North Sea sellers to find space in a crowded U.S. Gulf facing a flood of Nigerian crude.
Six or seven June Oseberg cargoes and a similar number of Statfjords were still looking for homes less than a week away from the release of July loading programmes.
"I see a lot of oil out there, not only in the North Sea but also in the Mediterranean so actually I don't see any good reason for an improvement in wet differentials," a second trader said.
Other North Sea grades like Forties, which lost 10-15 cents last week, and Dated Brent showed few signs of clambering out of the basement.

The benchmark grade traded at a discount of 49 cents to July forward paper on Friday and short-dated swaps or CFDs were indicating a value of July -50/-45 cents for the balance of this week on Monday.

July North Sea programmes should compound current bearish sentiment with volumes expected to jump after a heavy platform maintenance schedule this month but improving refinery margins may provide a glimmer of hope for producers.
Rotterdam and Mediterranean margins rallied 70 cents and nearly $1 a barrel respectively last week as crude tumbled.
The pressure of at least 15 million unsold June barrels is set to weigh heavily on the West African crude market this week, with differentials set to ease.
With time running out for FOB sales, most of the unsold oil has already been booked onto ships for transatlantic sailings, with three million unsold barrels already on the water.
"Most of the oil has ships underneath it. Some is already on the water and several VLCCs in the last decade have been booked onto ships but don't have destinations," said one trader.
Traders said sellers would have to drop prices sharply if the oil is to find homes in the U.S. Gulf.
Efforts by sellers to keep quotes artificially high until they sell barrels could encourage Nigerian National Petroleum Corp to set high July contract prices, one trader noted.
"If the NNPC prices don't reflect the market then it will just compound the problem and we'll see this weakness dragging on," he noted.
Bonny Light is expected to slip from Dated Brent plus mid-40s range this week, while Qua Iboe, having been displaced by Escravos in the last Indian tender was seen the weakest grade.

In the Mediterranean, Russian Urals recent strength based on a fairly tight prompt market is expected to ease with fresh exports of Iraqi Kirkuk crude under the renewed United Nations oil-for-food deal to start flowing in a couple of weeks.
Urals gained some 10 cents last week to trade at a high of around Dated Brent -$1.31, as most large first half June cargoes were snapped up amid better refining margins.
Traders said the June price of Kirkuk at around Dated Brent -$2.00 looked attractive relative to Urals but most agreed the downside was limited.
"I think there's a floor at (Dated Brent) -$1.40 for Urals," said one. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 7930
